name: Gaullism
summary: Gaullism is the French political current built around Charles de Gaulle's idea of national independence, a strong state and a powerful presidency standing above party quarrels. It favours state-guided economic growth, worker association with capital in place of class struggle, and a Europe of sovereign states, with an independent nuclear deterrent and military autonomy from the United States. It values French heritage and national unity.
scope: Classical Gaullism of de Gaulle and the early Fifth Republic, including its social-Gaullist strand (Capitant, Chaban-Delmas), based on the 1958 constitution, the Bayeux programme and scholarly accounts. Later neo-Gaullism (Chirac, Sarkozy), which moved toward liberalism and closer NATO ties, is not the baseline. Many issues beyond sovereignty, institutions and the economy are inferred and low confidence.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The Constitution makes the finance bill a parliamentary vote (Article 47) (s1).

class-collaboration.rationale: The RPF programme rejects class struggle for an 'association' of capital and labour with shared profits (s8).

collective-bargaining.rationale: He preferred contracts inside the firm to collective conventions, which he called armistices (s8).

consent-of-governed.rationale: At Epinal de Gaulle says the people must decide the institutions by referendum and rejects the tyranny of a man, group or party (s3).

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: De Gaulle put direct presidential election to the 1962 referendum, which was adopted (s7).

direct-votes.rationale: De Gaulle used Article 11 referendums, including 1962 (s7).

elective-rulers.rationale: The Constitution makes the presidency elective, by universal suffrage (s1).

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: De Gaulle kept the Atlantic alliance while the Soviet threat lasted (s5).

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Article 1 guarantees equality before the law to all citizens without distinction of origin, race or religion (s1).

head-commands-forces.rationale: Article 15 makes the President commander-in-chief of the armed forces (s1), and de Gaulle used that role (s7).

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Both speeches give the head of state the power to dissolve the Assembly, as arbiter in grave confusion (s2, s3).

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: De Gaulle built France's own nuclear force and refused NATO military integration (s6).

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: France built and kept its own nuclear force under de Gaulle (s6); the sources state no wider rule for other states.

multipolar-world.rationale: Gaullist foreign policy opposes two-bloc hegemony and seeks a multipolar world (s6).

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: De Gaulle's 1948 press conference says the old capitalism will not be kept as it was and communism is not wanted; association is the way out (s8).

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Scholarship records that France did not support foreign bases on its territory (s6).

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: De Gaulle's institutional speeches put a head of state above parties as national arbiter (s2, s3).

one-party-rule.rationale: De Gaulle rejects the tyranny of any party and calls party dominance the vice of the Fourth Republic (s3, s4).

pool-sovereignty.rationale: France under de Gaulle opposed supranational institutions (s6).

priority-to-poor.rationale: At Epinal he asks for attention first to the least advantaged (s3).

public-ownership.rationale: His government nationalised coal, electricity, credit and Renault, but he said there was no reason for some firms to stay nationalised for ever (s8).

second-chamber.rationale: Bayeux and Epinal both call for two chambers, the second elected by local councils and economic, family and intellectual bodies (s2, s3).

separate-church-state.rationale: De Gaulle held full independence of State and Church as a guarantee of mutual freedom (s7); Article 1 makes the Republic secular (s1).

separated-powers.rationale: In the Bayeux and Epinal speeches de Gaulle calls for separated, balanced powers, with the executive not issuing from parliament and justice independent (s2, s3).

single-common-good.rationale: De Gaulle's programme says particular interest must always yield to the general interest and condemns coalitions of interests (s8).

state-class-instrument.rationale: De Gaulle held the state to be the impartial supreme arbiter above parties and classes (s8).

state-directs-investment.rationale: De Gaulle says the state must hold the levers of energy, transport and credit so as to direct national savings toward large investments, linked to the Plan (s8).

state-harmful.rationale: De Gaulle defends 'un Etat juste et fort' and calls for a strong state (s3, s4).

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: De Gaulle called the two-camp division fading and wanted Europe to have its own policy, yet kept the Atlantic alliance while the Soviet threat lasted (s5): his words pull both ways.

strong-leader.rationale: Scholarship reports de Gaulle's strong executive of authority above parties, with the referendum, dissolution and Article 16 as tools (s7).

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Scholarship reports de Gaulle's view of French history as continuous, without ruptures (s7).

unions-good.rationale: De Gaulle said unions had done great service to workers while wanting them free of party control (s8).

women-suffrage.rationale: Article 3 makes suffrage universal, equal and open to both sexes (s1).

workplace-democracy.rationale: He asked for workers' association in firms' management and profits, but also insisted that the rights and authority of management be respected (s8).

notes: This second pass rebuilt the audit on de Gaulle's own speeches, the Constitution and scholarship, nulling answers that earlier rested on Wikipedia or inference. Neo-Gaullists (Chirac onward) accepted privatisation, closer NATO ties and, in part, European integration, and would answer the economic and Europe items differently. Searched without finding a stated position: proportional representation, organic representation, pronatalism, social-market economy.
